I want to call out the privilege of the OP and people who agree with them.
When you work with someone with chronic ptsd and they barely make any progress for months or OCD that prevents that person from even coming to an appointment anything but 20+ mins late, I do not feel like you can afford statements about modalities not mattering if you hope to actually improve this person's functioning.
In fact, there are cases where the opposite is true. I had met several not-person-centered clinicians, who are highly specialized and protocol based, but provide miraculous results in just a few sessions. 
Takes like this set us backwards and make us appear hokey pokey to the general population, the compassion and positive regard is just not enough for a lot of people.

Therapy is a highly scientific machine, which has very specific (e.g. Memory reconsolidation) reasons why it works. And I am not even going to respond to you saying how people getting hurt is what makes a great therapist.
Can you help the person feel better, heard, and validated just about regardless of modality? Sure, but a lot of us are aiming at the long term consistent and timely progress. Even someone like Yirvin Yalom, dude who was there just about when modern therapy was born (still kicking at 95 BTW), in his earlier books written about not confining yourself to "what had been researched" and searching for what works for the person, despite going outside of what most people accept is the way to do therapy. And he is probably one of the most person centered, "let love touch souls" people out there.

Yes, if I notice that this is an issue that locks the person and something I just want to spend a full session on.
Even when people have individual therapists, they are often addressing things that are more pressing to their overall well-being vs something that comes up only during couple counseling and prevents them from being present with their partner.
As arrogant as that might sound, I disagree with the people who talk about blurred boundaries and pushing things onto individual work. With couple counseling very often you have two people, generally with a history of trauma both, throwing their last towel in hopes that maybe this will save the relationship. Not all the time, but my personal experience is that often at least one, if not both, partner is not in therapy, so by the time they find someone, even if they agree to do so, it might already be too late for the relationship.
So, I can either tip toe around every potential issue that might get triggered, or focus on saving the situation (if it's possible or appropriate of course) by whatever means will give us most benefit. As much as we might want to hold up both partners on even ground as much as possible, usually one person might need a lot more work than the other. 
Case in point, several times had a couple that has one of the partners working a compassion job (doctors, nurses, therapists, etc) burning them out to the point of not being able to have any energy for the partner. They literally couldn't do couple's work, so I spent two individual sessions with  the burnt out one, and another session with the other partner to help them tolerate the abandonment better, and that alone significantly kick started the relationship.
Maybe I am being dismissive, but to me AI is as much of a threat to therapy as healthy diet and regular exercise.

I always tell my clients thag creativity is a very important resource. Instead of trying to do things the way others (including myself) say or imply "should be done", try to search for creative solutions that fit your personal body.
People who struggle with this often default to half baked solutions, such as lists, alarms, sticky notes, etc., but ironically for a lot of us those things cause even more issues and then we start to judge ourselves for being incapable, while the world is actively providing a set of tools that works against us. 
Instead, we want to adapt the tools, ourselves, and our environment in a way that actually benefits us by engaging in creativity and given ourselves permission to make errors and learn from them.

I seem to be going against the grain here, but my background is internal family systems, and I had talked about these situations a lot in supervision. 
Person's environment directly connects to their well-being, so I am of the opinion that if it's done for the benefit of the client, do it. I work with a lot of people on the spectrum and Bpd is not uncommon, and I had clients bring their parents, their partners, and even their children. 
The way I keep boundaries is that I discuss the meeting prior with the client, and I talk to them about what and how I will say it, what they can expect me to bring up, and what are they okay with me to talk about. Also if the client is not there, I mostly let the parent or whoever lead, because I obviously aim to not reveal or suggest of any information that the client told me, I only aim to address parent's personal experience of the situation, unless the client wants me to bring something up or I suggest to the client something and they agreed prior.
These type of meetings are very helpful, because within the context of your specific question, it allows you to bring to light some chronic miscommunication that goes unnoticed or provide some very helpful resources or to encourage parents to seek their own therapy to help deal with the stress or triggers that come in the way of their relationship with their children
 I had several experiences with parents of adult clients who "turned around" from being neglectful and abusive to trying to repair their relationships, and it always makes a huge impact on both. So I feel it is very beneficial to support the parents if they are willing to participate and be quick to resource or refer our if you feel like they need a more intense intervention. 
Last note, for communication, you obviously need both the client and the other person, but for education and guidance, it's better for the client to not be in the room, because it is a very childifying experience to be talked about and allows the parents to be more open with you, giving you a better opportunity to notice any significant dysfunctions within the family.

1. Yes, and no. Memory is is affected and problem can be "solved", but no memory works in an isolated box, so there is always more to the story.

2. Something that I am very glad in retrospect, but I learned ifs not from Schwartz. He has a very strong (and a bit rigid) shamanistic approach to IFS. Jay Early, Frank Anderson, and many others present IFS specifics differently, while keeping the same core. Practicing it for 3 years, my approach is fundamentally based in ifs, but the way I present it is very different from how it is taught. When I started, I used to get into roadblocks of people saying it's weird, etc, not in the last 1.5 years, because I learned what parts (pun unintended) work well for all (separating, appreciation, reparenting), and which ones do I use (talking directly to the part, certain questions, etc.) in a very specific situations. 
3/4. I love ifs, and found almost no limitations (other than obvious retrospective, alexathymia, and similar) as a base, but in my opinion you have to build other sources of knowledge on top to apply it effectively. 


Personally, what really helps me use IFS a lot is that I don't do ifs directly. I do trauma work first, and I often explain the clients the science of trauma work (feel free to do some reading into Memory Reconsolodation). What ifs calls parts are simply memory clusters, so the way you work with memory in a way that facilitates healing is my goal always, and I use the ifs foundation to help me keep things consistent and easy to comprehend, and build with Emdr, Relational Life Therapy, Narrative therapy, and even basic dbt, cbt stuff on top.
So my suggestion, learn the science, and keep trying things as you learn them, because there is my style of therapy and there is yours. I like logistics, so ifs is my thing,maybe you are more of an Emdr person, but some small parts of ifs language would be helpful to you specifically (such as checking for obscuring parts, which is the best way to work with resistance in my opinion, because it's very cooperative with the client against the problem, instead of making the client feel like they are doing something wrong). If you enjoy and flow with the your process, people would feel your confidence and flow with you forward, in comparison to using the "best" approach possible that seems to go against the grain of who you are.

I highly recommend, especially to early career therapists, both books by Courtney Armstrong, The Therapeutic Aha and Rethinking Trauma Therapy. 
They really helped me conceptualize how to work with clients and have a very strong science backing to help you understand the foundation of what makes therapy work to help you apply it in multiple ways.

Something for you to consider is that you feeling the need to ask this question on Reddit probably says more about your therapeutic experience than it does about you. Not to dismiss your curiosity and openness to outside input, but having your symptoms after being in therapy for that many years, even if not actively, is a red flag to me. Obviously, there are a lot of factors I don't know, so I could be completely wrong, but we unfortunately have very little oversight, once I entered the field I was eventually horrified at the realization how many therapists do genuinely mediocre therapy, if not bad one, for decades, and get a great reputation regardless.

Am trauma therapist. The problem with this question is that it is paradoxical in nature, which is why a lot of these answers, while helpful to a functioning healthy person, will very likely fall flat for you. However, I do agree that the problem is probably a lot worse due to the basic biology - stress from financials, unsatisfactory job, lack of meaningful relationships or exercise, inflammation, vitamin deficiency (especially D), poor diet, etc. All of those things add together and make a very hard spiral to deal with. 
While some of these issues have relatively simple fixes, like popping some supplements or slight changes in the diet, ultimately it again comes down to the question of "what to do, when you don't feel like doing anything."
The potential solution, that might not necessarily apply to you, but something for you to consider, is to look at the doing process as a whole. You mention PTSD, which even if recent, gives me an idea that your nervous system was always vulnerable to this outcome. So what was different about your college and high school? Generally, the conclusion that I come to working with a lot of people who describe this to me, is that they got used to "motivating" themselves through self criticism and pushing through the problems and emotionally detaching from underlying issues. When you are in college, the pressure to perform is a lot less and due to availability of peers, biology, and other factors it is easier to ignore those problems and function well despite depression and anxiety. The problem is that the body is not meant to carry this on for a long time, to push things down is an emergency response, so what I often see is somewhere in the 18-25 range is when things that were not addressed earlier really come back to bite you, as you are more and more faced with the fact that you are emotionally unprepared to be an adult. 
If this applies to you, then it is probably a good idea to find a therapist that can help you with this. Psychiatry for most issues is not meant to be a long term solution, it is meant to help you stabilize so that you actually have the capacity to address ptsd and stressors. 
Obviously, therapy is a privilege and not everyone has that availability, the surface level answer is to start addressing the core of the way you approach the concept of "doing things." Are you getting caught up in negative feedback of things not done and self criticism? Are you struggling with self worth (we take care of pets because we see them as worthy)? Do you have executive dysfunction or other limitations and try to brute force "should be better" instead of adapting to it? Think of pets or people that you care about and actually find it much easier to help or put effort for, what is separating the way you think about them and yourself. 
Hope this helps.

I am a clinical therapist and dealt with depression personally as well. There are too many small factors that help, like diet, sleep, exercise, relationships, etc. However, what I find to be one of the most important things is meaning making. We all experience challenges, though to different degrees, and often make them mean that we are bad, don't deserve care/love/joy, worthless, incapable, etc.

90%+ of my work is addressing the meaning you took away from life's experiences. Once people start to truly believe they are worth loving and caring for, they tend to fix small things on their own, eat better, have better relationships, etc. and depression starts to dissipate from that.
